title: Preparing a marketing plan: mission, present position and goals before channels
audience: Owners of service businesses who are about to write a marketing plan and need the thinking done before they choose channels, budgets or activities.
referencesAtStart: Official source: business.gov.au, Develop your marketing plan (page metadata date 26 February 2026; no last-updated date is shown on the page; checked by direct fetch 2026-11-03). The planning stages below are reworded from a published marketing planning workbook. The workbook is not quoted, and no figures from it are used.
learningOutcomes: Write a short mission statement that says why the business exists, and test it against one real decision the business faces.
Describe the present position of a service business using facts, and separate each fact from an opinion.
State the basic assumptions the marketing plan depends on, and set a measurable goal before choosing any channel.

instruction.heading: Why preparation comes before the plan
instruction.body: A good marketing plan depends more on the work done before writing than on the writing itself. A plan written without that work tends to list activities that do not connect to the business's purpose or its limits, so it is hard to act on and hard to measure. The preparation has four parts: a mission, an honest view of the present position, a set of basic assumptions, and goals. Only when these are clear should you choose channels, budgets and activities. Those are covered in the marketing plan template lesson, which is the next step after this one.

instruction.heading: A mission that can settle a decision
instruction.body: A mission statement says, briefly, why the business exists and whom it serves. Keep it short enough to say aloud. A useful test is whether the mission would help you choose between two real options. For example, a business whose mission is to keep local homes safe and clean would decline a job it cannot do safely, even if the job pays well. A mission that cannot separate two options is too vague to guide a plan. Write it in plain words, and avoid slogans that could describe any business at all.

instruction.heading: Present position: facts before opinions
instruction.body: Before you plan, describe where the business stands, using questions that have answers you can check. What is the financial position? What do competitors charge and offer? How do existing clients describe the business? Which markets will you target, and which can you reach? Mark each answer as a fact, from your records or a checked source, or as an opinion, such as a belief about the market. When a fact and an opinion conflict, the fact wins. Where the answer is not known, write it down as a gap, and give a date by which it will be filled.

instruction.heading: Basic assumptions that limit the plan
instruction.body: Make the assumptions behind the plan explicit. Decide whether the business is an innovator, which creates a new service to meet a new need, or an imitator, which improves a service that already works for others. Set the geographic limits you can serve well, and count the cost of travel and time within those limits, because a distant job can cost more than it earns. Write down any other assumption the plan depends on, such as the number of jobs per week, the price per job, or the availability of staff. Give each assumption a date and an owner, so it can be checked later. Check the assumptions about buyers against research before you rely on them. The Victorian Government's 'Who is my customer?' guidance suggests comparing how many competitors exist, how often buyers need the service and where they prefer to buy.

instruction.heading: Goals and measures before channels
instruction.body: A goal states a result to reach by a date, such as a number of new bookings from referrals within six months. A goal is useful only if you can measure it, which means a baseline, a target, a date and a data source. Set few goals, with one or two measures for each. Only then choose the channels and activities that support each goal. A channel chosen before its goal is hard to judge, because nothing says what success looks like. When the plan is running, review the goals on a fixed date, keep what works, and change what does not.

procedure: Write the mission in two or three sentences, and test it against a real decision the business has faced or may face.
List the facts about the present position, and mark each one as a fact with its source or as an opinion.
Write the basic assumptions: innovator or imitator, geographic limits, travel cost, jobs per week and staff availability.
Set one or two goals, each with a baseline, a target, a date and a data source.
Only then choose the channels and activities for each goal, and link each one to the marketing plan template.
Set the review date, and write what result would mean keep, change or stop.

workedExamples.situation: EXAMPLE, invented for teaching and not from a real business: a two-person home-service business wants more bookings from repeat clients. Its records show 12 jobs last month, of which 3 came from repeat clients.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which part of the preparation is missing if the owner starts by choosing a social media campaign?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner has skipped the goal. A goal could be to raise repeat jobs from the current baseline to a stated target within six months, using the same booking records as the data source. The baseline in this example is 3 repeat jobs out of 12, which is 25 per cent. With that goal, the owner can judge a campaign by whether repeat jobs rise, and can compare it with a reminder system, a loyalty offer or a referral request. The present position should also say whether the team can take more jobs without a new hire, and the assumptions should state the travel limit for the suburbs served.

equipmentAndPpe: A notebook or document for the mission, the present position and the list of assumptions.
Job and booking records for the last three months.
No personal protective equipment is needed for this desk-based lesson.

commonErrors.error: Writing a mission that could describe any business.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the test: would the mission change one real decision the business has to make?

commonErrors.error: Mixing opinions with facts in the present position.
commonErrors.prevention: Mark each statement as a fact with a source, or as an opinion that needs checking.

commonErrors.error: Choosing channels before setting a goal.
commonErrors.prevention: Set the goal, with a baseline and a target, first, and then choose the channels.
Write each assumption with a date and an owner, so it can be tested.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Businesses must not mislead consumers, and marketing claims should be true, accurate and based on reasonable grounds (ACCC guidance on false or misleading claims, read 2026-11-04). Messages to customers must follow ACMA's spam guidance, which requires consent, sender identification and a working unsubscribe (read 2026-11-03). If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to the business, its privacy rules apply as well; check the OAIC's small business guidance to see whether it does.
The business.gov.au guidance on marketing plans is general. It is not a substitute for advice on a specific business, its licences or its tax position.

qualityStandard: The mission is written in two or three sentences and has been tested against one real decision.
Every statement in the present position is marked as a fact with a source and date, or as an opinion.
Each basic assumption has a date and an owner.
Each goal has a baseline, a target, a date and a data source before any channel is chosen.
documentationEvidence: Written mission, present position and assumption list, each dated and with an owner.
Goal sheet with the baseline, the target, the date and the data source for each goal.
summary: A marketing plan depends on preparation: the mission, the present position, the assumptions and the goals come first.
Facts override opinions, and each assumption needs a date and an owner.
Choose channels only after each goal has a baseline and a target.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which comes first in a marketing plan?
options: The channels and the budget and the staff rota for the year
The mission and an honest view of the present position
The social media posts and the printed flyers for the street

knowledgeChecks.question: A present-position note says "our clients love us". What should you do with it?
options: Write it down as a fact, because clients are the best judge
Mark it as an opinion, and look for a record or a check that supports it
Keep it as a fact, since a client's opinion proves the claim

knowledgeChecks.question: A goal reads: get more repeat clients. What is missing to make it measurable?
options: A colour scheme for the business and the logo design
A list of every channel to be used and the cost of each one
A baseline, a target number, a date and a data source
